strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: unreliable minority-class pseudo-labels in semi-supervised graph learning. Combining clustering agreement, geometric ranking, and ambiguity filtering is a practical, modular approach.

The experimental coverage is substantial, including multiple GNN backbones, synthetic and natural imbalance, large graphs, and heterophilous benchmarks. Several reported improvements are meaningful; Table 20 reports Cora-GCN macro-F1 of 76.44 versus 72.67 for the strongest listed baseline at imbalance ratio 10.

The appendix provides useful diagnostics of pseudo-label accuracy, including separate minority-class analyses, component comparisons, and sensitivity studies. These offer empirical support for improving pseudo-label selection.

Public benchmarks, a code URL, pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, and hardware details provide a useful foundation for reproduction. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described study.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is false as stated. With two antipodal class centers, equal concentration parameters, and fixed unequal priors, moving a minority embedding from an equidistant direction toward the wrong center increases its geometric imbalance while eventually decreasing prediction entropy. Appendix C also drops the class priors and class-specific concentrations from the stated posterior. Its final sandwich bounds contradict each other when D_intra = 0. These problems invalidate the central claimed entropy–geometry relationship.

Theorem 2 conflates labeled-set imbalance with neighborhood composition. Changing which labels are observed need not change graph neighborhoods or embeddings under a fixed extractor. No graph-generation or learning assumptions establish the asserted dependence of neighbor mixing on the imbalance ratio. Appendix D additionally asserts proportionality to rho squared and then concludes proportionality to rho without justification.

The connection between the theory and algorithm remains unestablished. Definition 1 measures distance to the true class center relative to global separation, whereas DGIS measures separation between the two nearest centroids; confidently misclassified nodes can have high formal imbalance and still pass DGIS. The vMF analysis also does not establish guarantees for the implemented MLP classifier. Theorem 3 only demonstrates a weighting property, not reduced imbalance; moreover, the confidence weight min(r, 1-r) decreases once r exceeds 0.5, contrary to the general narrative.

The ablation reporting is internally inconsistent. In Tables 1 and 32, every best-F1 row marks both Node-Reordering and DGIS as absent, while the text credits their combination with the best results. The component mappings must be corrected before their contributions can be assessed. Claims of consistently outperforming all baselines also overstate the results: Table 4 reports lower balanced accuracy and F1 for GraphSAGE on Computers-Random.

Originality relative to the closest methods needs clearer delineation. Appendix B acknowledges that M3S already filters pseudo-labels using clustering/classifier agreement, closely resembling DPAM. Its comparison is restricted to CS-Random in Table 19, leaving the incremental contribution under severe imbalance insufficiently isolated. IceBerg, a directly relevant 2025 self-training method discussed in the paper, is absent from the experimental comparisons.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence remain incomplete for the broader claims. Appendix K omits detailed ogbn-arxiv/products-specific selection and training configurations. Table 12 measures training for fixed epoch counts and selecting 100 nodes, while the actual method can use 40–100 rounds with up to 2000 epochs per round; this does not establish end-to-end efficiency against competing methods. The manuscript also inconsistently describes uncertainty as standard errors versus standard deviations. Together with the central theoretical and ablation problems, these concerns outweigh the promising empirical results.
